john-collins: The Collins began in London as a gin punch associated with John Collins, headwaiter at Limmer's Old House on Conduit Street in Mayfair in the early 1800s, whose name survives in a rhyme about him. In America the drink split in two, and by the 1880s bar manuals such as Harry Johnson's gave a Tom Collins made with sweetened Old Tom gin and a John Collins made with Dutch gin. The names have been used loosely ever since, and in many American bars a John Collins now means the same drink made with whiskey.
paradise: The Paradise first appears in print in 1922, in Harry MacElhone's Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails and in Robert Vermeire's Cocktails: How to Mix Them, as a mix of gin, apricot brandy and orange juice. Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 set the version most bartenders follow, two parts gin to one each of apricot brandy and orange juice. Nobody recorded who first mixed it or why it was called Paradise, and the apricot brandy of these recipes means a sweet apricot liqueur rather than a dry distilled spirit.
pink-gin: Pink Gin is generally traced to the officers of the Royal Navy in the nineteenth century. Angostura bitters, created by Dr Johann Siegert in the Venezuelan town of Angostura, were carried aboard ship as a supposed remedy for seasickness, and a few dashes in a glass of Plymouth gin, long carried on Royal Navy ships, turned the gin pink. The habit came ashore to British clubs and bars, along with the old choice of keeping the bitters in the glass or swirling them out before the gin goes in.
russian-spring-punch: Dick Bradsell created the Russian Spring Punch in London in the 1980s, for friends who wanted to throw a cocktail party but were short of money. He had each guest bring a bottle of champagne and set out glasses already built with vodka, lemon, sugar, crème de cassis and ice, ready to be topped up. He later explained the name simply: vodka for Russia, and a long fizz of the kind he thought of as a spring drink.
snakebite: Snakebite, equal parts lager and cider, has no recorded inventor, but it was a familiar order in British pubs and student bars by the 1980s, often with a dash of blackcurrant cordial as a Snakebite and Black. A persistent myth holds that it is illegal in the United Kingdom; it is not, though some pubs have house rules against serving it.
snowball: The Snowball, Dutch advocaat lengthened with lemonade and a squeeze of lime, is a long-standing fixture of British Christmas gatherings, and no creator or date is on record.
treacle: Dick Bradsell, the bartender behind much of London's cocktail revival, created the Treacle in London in the 1990s as a twist on the Old Fashioned. He built it in the glass with dark rum, sugar and bitters, adding the ice a little at a time and stirring between additions, then finished it with a float of apple juice. He is reported to have used plain clear apple juice rather than the cloudy pressed kind, and the name suits the dark, molasses-rich drink in the glass.
whisky-mac: The Whisky Mac pairs Scotch with green ginger wine, and its name is traditionally explained by a Colonel Hector Macdonald, who is said to have first mixed the two while serving in India under the British Raj. The story is popular but unproven. The usual ginger wine is Stone's, a London brand with eighteenth-century roots, and the mix became a standard winter order in Scottish and British pubs.
white-lady: Harry MacElhone made the first drink called the White Lady at Ciro's Club in London in 1919, but it was built on crème de menthe rather than gin. The gin, triple sec and lemon recipe known today has two claimants: MacElhone is said to have rebuilt it with gin at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in 1929, while the Savoy credits Harry Craddock, who printed the gin version in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930. The early recipes have no egg white, which became a common addition later.
wibble: Dick Bradsell created the Wibble in 1999 at The Player in Soho for Nick Blacknell, a well-known gin enthusiast, and built it on Plymouth gin and sloe gin with grapefruit, lemon and a little crème de mûre. He named it after Weebles, the roly-poly children's toys of the 1970s, whose advertising promised that they wobbled but did not fall down. It is counted among his modern London classics alongside the Bramble and the Russian Spring Punch.
alaska: The Alaska appears in the 1910s in the bar manuals of Jacques Straub, made with Old Tom gin, yellow Chartreuse and orange bitters. By the time Harry Craddock printed it in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930 it had become a drier mix of dry gin and Chartreuse, with a joking note that it was not the staple diet of Arctic peoples and had probably first been thought of in South Carolina. No one knows who named it, or why.
between-the-sheets: Between the Sheets has a disputed birth. It is often credited to Harry MacElhone of Harry's New York Bar in Paris, while another account places it at the Berkeley hotel in London around 1921, and a third story places it in French brothels. The equal parts of brandy, rum and triple sec with a dash of lemon that bartenders follow today match the recipe Harry Craddock printed in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930, which makes it a Sidecar with a second spirit added.
bijou: The Bijou dates to the 1890s and is credited to Harry Johnson, the New York bartender who printed it in the 1900 edition of his Bartenders' Manual: equal parts Plymouth gin, green Chartreuse and Italian vermouth, with orange bitters. The name is French for jewel, explained by the colours of the three ingredients, gin for diamond, Chartreuse for emerald and vermouth for ruby. The drink faded after Prohibition until Dale DeGroff found it in Johnson's book in the 1980s and revived it with more gin.
blue-blazer: Jerry Thomas made the Blue Blazer his signature: Scotch whisky and boiling water set alight and tossed between two mugs in a flaming arc. By most accounts he developed it in San Francisco during the gold rush, at the El Dorado gambling saloon, and he printed it in his Bar-Tender's Guide of 1862, often called the first American bar book. Thomas himself advised beginners to practise the pour for some time with cold water, and the trick made his name as a showman.
boilermaker: A shot of whiskey served with a glass of beer, the Boilermaker is usually said to be named for the industrial boilermakers who ordered it after a shift, though no one has documented where or when the name began.
bronx: The Bronx was one of the most famous drinks in America by the early 1900s, and more than one man claimed it. Johnnie Solon, a bartender at the old Waldorf-Astoria, told the hotel's historian Albert Stevens Crockett that he mixed it there and named it after a recent visit to the Bronx Zoo. Joseph Sormani, a Bronx restaurateur, was also credited with it, including in his New York Times obituary, and an earlier mention of a Bronx cocktail on a New York hotel menu leaves Solon's account in doubt.
brooklyn: The Brooklyn cocktail that survives first appeared in print around 1908 in Jack's Manual, by Jacob Grohusko, a bartender at Baracca's restaurant in New York, as rye, vermouth, maraschino and Amer Picon. Jacques Straub's Drinks of 1914 and The Savoy Cocktail Book printed it with dry vermouth, which became the standard. Amer Picon's scarcity in the United States kept the drink obscure for decades, and its revival in New York bars inspired a run of variations named after other Brooklyn neighbourhoods.
cable-car: Tony Abou-Ganim created the Cable Car in 1996 as the signature drink of the Starlight Room, the bar on the 21st floor of San Francisco's Sir Francis Drake Hotel. He built it on Captain Morgan spiced rum with orange liqueur and lemon and gave it a cinnamon-sugar rim, which makes it a spiced relative of the Sidecar and of the older Brandy Crusta. The name nods to the cable cars that run along Powell Street past the hotel, and it remains his best-known original drink.
casino: The Casino is first recorded in Jacob A. Didier's The Reminder of 1909, and Hugo Ensslin printed it in his Recipes for Mixed Drinks in 1916 as Old Tom gin with dashes of maraschino, orange bitters and lemon juice. Harry Craddock carried it into The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930. It is a close cousin of the Aviation without the violet, and no one recorded where its name came from.
eggnog: Eggnog is generally thought to descend from posset, the hot spiced drink of milk curdled with wine or ale that was popular in Britain from medieval times, and the word eggnog is first recorded in the American colonies in 1775, in a poem by a Maryland clergyman. Where the nog came from is disputed, with candidates including noggin, a small wooden cup, and nog, an old East Anglian name for a strong beer. In America the drink took on rum, brandy or whiskey and became a fixture of the Christmas season.
french-connection: A two-ingredient pairing of cognac and amaretto from the same family as the Godfather and the Godmother, the French Connection has no recorded creator, and its name is generally taken from the crime film of the same name.
godfather: The Godfather, Scotch and amaretto over ice, is generally dated to the 1970s, and its name is usually taken from the 1972 film, though no one has documented who first mixed it. Disaronno, the amaretto brand, has long said it was Marlon Brando's favourite cocktail, a claim that belongs to the drink's lore rather than its record. It is part of a family of spirit and amaretto pairs that includes the Godmother and the French Connection, and it was on the International Bartenders Association's official list from at least 1987 until 2020.
golden-dream: The Golden Dream is usually credited to Raimundo Alvarez, a bartender at the Old King Bar in Miami, who is said to have dedicated it to the actress Joan Crawford. Its mix of Galliano, triple sec, orange juice and cream became popular along the American East Coast in the late 1960s and through the 1970s, when Galliano's tall bottle was a fixture on back bars. The International Bartenders Association had it on its official list by 1987 and dropped it in 2024.
greenpoint: Michael McIlroy created the Greenpoint at Milk & Honey in New York in the mid-2000s and named it after the Brooklyn neighbourhood of Greenpoint. It followed the Red Hook in a run of Manhattan variations named for Brooklyn neighbourhoods, all descended from the old Brooklyn cocktail, and it uses rye, sweet vermouth and yellow Chartreuse with Angostura and orange bitters. It has become one of the best known drinks of the series.
horses-neck: The Horse's Neck was being served in American bars by the 1890s as a soft drink: ginger ale over ice with a long spiral of lemon peel curling from the glass, the garnish that gave it its name. Spirit came later, ordered at first as a Horse's Neck with a kick or a stiff Horse's Neck, until the name came to mean the spiked version. Bourbon became the American choice, while brandy took over in Britain, where the drink became a favourite of Royal Navy wardrooms.
hot-buttered-rum: Putting butter into hot drinks is an old British habit, with buttered ale and beer recipes going back centuries, and in colonial New England, where rum was distilled from Caribbean molasses, the habit met the local spirit. Recipes long stayed in families rather than in print, and Jerry Thomas's pioneering bar guide gave a hot spiced rum of sugar, Jamaica rum, allspice, cloves and a piece of butter topped with hot water. The drink found new fans in the middle of the twentieth century, when Trader Vic recommended making it from a spiced butter batter.
illegal: The Illegal's history is thin. One account, not independently confirmed, credits an Italian hotel bartender in the Veneto in the late 1990s, who began with a Daiquiri variation on tequila and later switched it to mezcal. What is certain is that the International Bartenders Association added it to its official list in 2020, with mezcal, overproof Jamaican rum, falernum, maraschino and lime.
jasmine: Paul Harrington created the Jasmine in the 1990s while bartending at the Townhouse in Emeryville, across the bay from San Francisco, and named it after Matt Jasmin, a friend from architecture school, misspelling the name as he did. He built it as a variation on the Pegu Club, the drink he most liked to recommend, using Campari in place of bitters and lemon in place of lime, with gin and Cointreau. It spread after Harrington included it in his 1998 book, and its grapefruit-like taste comes from no grapefruit at all.
lava-flow: A frozen Hawaiian resort drink of rum, coconut and pineapple poured over strawberry purée, the Lava Flow has no recorded creator or date, and its name simply describes the red streaks that rise through the glass.
little-italy: Audrey Saunders created the Little Italy in 2005 at Pegu Club, the bar she co-founded on West Houston Street in New York, as a Manhattan variation that adds Cynar, the Italian artichoke-based amaro, to rye and sweet vermouth. The name nods to the Italian neighbourhood near the bar and to the mix of American and Italian ingredients in the glass. It arrived as Cynar was beginning to find a place in American cocktail bars, and it remains one of the most familiar drinks built on it.
pisco-punch: Duncan Nicol made the Pisco Punch famous in the 1890s at the Bank Exchange saloon on Montgomery Street in San Francisco, where pisco punches had already been served under earlier owners. Pisco, the grape brandy of Peru and Chile, had been reaching the city by ship since before the gold rush, and Nicol kept his recipe secret until Prohibition closed the saloon in 1919. In 1973 a California Historical Society article claimed to reveal the recipe, built on pisco, pineapple, citrus and gum syrup.
remember-the-maine: Charles H. Baker Jr. recorded the Remember the Maine after a night in Havana during the revolution of 1933, and printed it in The Gentleman's Companion in 1939: rye, sweet vermouth, cherry brandy and a little absinthe. The name recalls the USS Maine, the American battleship whose sinking in Havana harbour helped start the Spanish-American War, and Baker told readers to stir it clockwise with a long spoon. In 2024 the International Bartenders Association added it to its official list.
revolver: Jon Santer created the Revolver in 2004 while working at Bruno's in San Francisco, as a simple twist on the Manhattan built on Bulleit bourbon, then a new arrival that bartenders were excited about, with coffee liqueur, orange bitters and a flamed orange peel. He later took the drink to Bourbon & Branch, where the theatre of the flamed twist made it a frequent order and helped carry it to bars far beyond the city.
rob-roy: The Rob Roy is usually credited to a bartender at the Waldorf Hotel in New York in 1894 and is named after Rob Roy, an operetta by Reginald De Koven and Harry B. Smith about the Scottish outlaw Rob Roy MacGregor, which was then playing at the nearby Herald Square Theatre. It is a Manhattan made with Scotch in place of rye, and it has kept its place on hotel bar menus ever since.
salty-dog: The Salty Dog is the salt-rimmed relative of the Greyhound, gin and grapefruit juice, which a Harper's Magazine article at the end of the Second World War described being served at the Post House restaurants in Greyhound bus terminals. No one recorded who first salted the rim to make a separate drink, and after the war vodka increasingly took the place of gin in both. The salt is there for flavour as well as looks, since it softens the bitterness of the grapefruit.
siesta: Katie Stipe created the Siesta at Flatiron Lounge in New York in 2006 as a riff on the Hemingway Daiquiri, with tequila in place of rum and Campari in place of maraschino, alongside lime and grapefruit. It arrived when American cocktail bars were only beginning to treat tequila as a serious base spirit, and it has since travelled well beyond the bar where it began.
southside: The Southside's origin is contested. Hugo Ensslin printed a South Side in his Recipes for Mixed Drinks in New York in 1916, which makes the popular story tying it to Prohibition Chicago, where rough gin supposedly needed mint and sugar to hide it, hard to accept. Long Island's Southside Sportsmen's Club is the other claimant, and Manhattan's 21 Club later made the mix of gin, citrus, sugar and mint one of its house drinks.
stinger: Brandy and crème de menthe were being shaken together in American bars by the 1890s, under names such as the Judge, printed in William Schmidt's The Flowing Bowl in 1892. The Stinger name was in print by the early 1900s, and the drink became a fashionable after-dinner order in New York society, with stories crediting the millionaire Reginald Vanderbilt with making it popular. It stayed a familiar nightcap through the middle of the century before fading in the 1970s, and it has returned with the classic cocktail revival.
stone-fence: Rum and hard cider were everyday drinks in eighteenth-century New England, and mixing the two is one of the plainest of early American drinks. Vermont legend says Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys drank it at a tavern in Castleton before they seized Fort Ticonderoga in 1775, a story long repeated but hard to verify. By the time Jerry Thomas printed the Stone Fence in his bar guide of 1862 it was bourbon and sweet cider, and no one recorded how it got its name.
tom-and-jerry: The Tom and Jerry takes its name from Corinthian Tom and Jerry Hawthorn, the young men about town in Pierce Egan's Life in London of the early 1820s and the stage play made from it. Jerry Thomas, who printed the drink in his bar guide of 1862, is often credited with inventing it, but its name was borrowed from a book published before he was born. It became an American Christmas custom, a batter of eggs, sugar and spice ladled into mugs with rum or brandy and hot milk or water, and it is still a winter tradition in parts of the upper Midwest.
tuxedo: The Tuxedo takes its name from the Tuxedo Club in Tuxedo Park, New York, the private club founded in the 1880s that also gave its name to the tailless dinner jacket. Recipes under the name were in American bar books by the 1910s, built on gin and dry vermouth with dashes of maraschino, absinthe and bitters, and the books never fully agreed on the details. The Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 printed two numbered versions, and the drink sits close to both the Martini and the Turf.
twelve-mile-limit: The Twelve Mile Limit is a drink of the 1920s, named for the line at sea where American Prohibition stopped being enforced. Liquor ships had waited just beyond the old three-mile limit until a 1924 treaty with Britain, followed by similar agreements with other nations, pushed the enforceable line out to about an hour's sailing from the coast, roughly twelve miles, and the drink took its name from the new boundary.
widows-kiss: The Widow's Kiss first appears in George Kappeler's Modern American Drinks of 1895, written while he was head bartender at the Holland House hotel in New York: apple brandy shaken with yellow Chartreuse, Bénédictine and Angostura bitters. Kappeler's book recorded many drinks for the first time, and nothing in it explains the name. The Widow's Kiss fell out of use after Prohibition and returned with the modern interest in pre-Prohibition recipes.
medio-y-medio: Medio y medio, half sweet sparkling wine and half dry white wine, is Uruguay's traditional aperitif, and its best-known version carries the name of Roldós, a restaurant that opened in Montevideo's Mercado del Puerto in the late 1880s and claims to have invented the mix. Roldós made it by hand for decades, and its bottled version is now produced for it by a Uruguayan winery, while other brands make their own. White was the original, and rosé and red versions are now made as well.
guarapita: Guarapita is a Venezuelan party mix of cane spirit or rum with fruit juice and sugar, most often passion fruit, made by the jug at home and at the beach, and no creator or date is on record.
ponche-crema: Ponche crema was put on the market in Caracas in 1900 by Eliodoro González P., a Venezuelan chemist and perfumer, as a bottled liqueur of milk, eggs, sugar and spirit, and its first known advertisement ran in the magazine El Cojo Ilustrado in 1905. Where the recipe itself came from is not known, and the formula of the brand, still sold under his name, remains a trade secret. It is Venezuela's Christmas drink, much as eggnog is in the United States, and many families still make their own at home with rum and nutmeg.
ruou-ran: Rượu rắn, rice spirit steeped with a whole snake, is Vietnam's form of the snake wine found across much of East and Southeast Asia, a tradition generally traced back to ancient China.
adonis: The Adonis is named after Adonis, the burlesque starring Henry E. Dixey that opened in New York in 1884 and became the first Broadway show to pass 500 performances. The drink, dry sherry and sweet vermouth with orange bitters, is said to have been mixed in honour of that long run, though no bartender is recorded as its creator. Jacques Straub's Drinks of 1914 and The Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 both printed it, and it has returned as bartenders have rediscovered sherry.
chrysanthemum: The Chrysanthemum first appears in Hugo Ensslin's Recipes for Mixed Drinks, published in New York in 1916: dry vermouth with Bénédictine and a few dashes of absinthe, and no base spirit at all. Harry Craddock included it in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930 with a note that it was well known and very popular in the American Bar of the SS Europa, a German transatlantic liner. No one recorded why it was named after the flower.
diplomat: The Diplomat appears in bar books of the early 1920s as a mix of dry and sweet vermouth with a dash of maraschino. Robert Vermeire, a Belgian bartender working in London, printed it in 1922 and noted that it was very well known in the French diplomatic service, which may explain the name. Harry Craddock repeated it in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930, and it belongs to the family of low-strength vermouth cocktails that were common in the early twentieth century.
cynar-julep: Dushan Zaric, an owner of the New York bar Employees Only, has described creating his Cynar Julep on a hot July day, when he wanted a long drink to enjoy with food and built a julep on Cynar, the Italian artichoke amaro, in place of bourbon. He added grapefruit, lemon and mint and finished it with a pinch of ras el hanout, the Moroccan spice blend, borrowed from the kitchen's spice rack. Cynar and grapefruit is also a familiar pairing in Argentina, where the amaro is made locally.
